intro: Two emails can say exactly the same thing and still land completely differently: one sounds warm and confident, the other cold, nervous or quietly annoyed. In this lesson you'll set your tone precisely, keep one consistent voice with good rhythm and precise words, and rewrite one message for very different readers. Warm-up: think of an email that annoyed you even though every word in it was polite.
teachingNotes: Recap the chain in one line, don't re-teach: c1-register (the formal / neutral / informal scale, chosen by audience, channel and purpose; don't mix registers), c1-connotation (same meaning, different feeling: slim / skinny; precise words for good / big), c2-grammar-for-style (end-focus, varying sentence length, a short sentence after long ones), c2-implied-meaning (the polite code: I'm not sure that's the best idea = I disagree) and c2-idiomatic-mastery (idioms in conversation, plain words in reports). New here: TONE as several dials, not just formality; tone that backfires; a consistent VOICE; rhythm and precise verbs; rewriting one message for very different readers. At C2 all grammar is available: the point is control and choice.

Objective adjust-style-and. Tone = the writer's attitude to the reader and the subject (nada tulisan). Five dials: formal–casual, warm–cool, confident–tentative, serious–playful, direct–indirect. Levers: word choice (we can't / we are unable to), sentence length, contractions, personal pronouns (we / you vs the company / customers, the passive), hedges (perhaps, might, just, I was wondering), punctuation (one ! = friendly; !!! = shouting or childish at work; a dash = a conversational aside; '...' = trailing off, reluctance; a one-word reply with a full stop, 'Fine.', can read as cold in chat). Tone that backfires: the defensive non-apology (We're sorry you feel …; sorry if …; However, as clearly stated …) and passive-aggressive phrases (pasif-agresif: annoyance hidden behind polite words): As per my last email = I already told you, read it; Just a gentle reminder / Friendly reminder (especially the second time) = you're late and I'm annoyed; Not sure if you saw my previous email = you ignored me; As I'm sure you're aware = you should know this; Going forward, please … = don't do that again; Thanks in advance = I expect you to do it. Say honestly that these are tendencies: some people use them innocently, but many readers hear the sting, so a C2 writer avoids them unless the sting is intended. The fix: neutral and specific (Could you send the figures by 3 p.m.? I need them for the board pack.).

Indonesian traps for tone: Indonesian moves tone with particles (ya, dong, sih, kok, deh) and English has none, so learners reach for !!! or emoji instead; 'Mohon' and 'Dengan hormat' become stiff 'Kindly …' / 'Please be informed'; 'As per' feels like neutral formal English to many Indonesian writers (from 'sesuai dengan'), but 'As per my last email' carries the same sting as 'Seperti yang sudah saya sampaikan sebelumnya'; 'Mohon maaf atas ketidaknyamanannya' becomes the empty 'We apologise for any inconvenience'; stacking hedges out of sungkan (I just wanted to maybe ask if possibly …) makes a confident proposal sound unsure. 'Sekadar mengingatkan' is fine in Indonesian; in English one neutral reminder is fine too, but the same phrase repeated or after a missed deadline reads as irritation.

Objective rhythm-word-choice. Voice = the stable personality of a writer or brand; tone = what shifts with the situation (Mailchimp's style guide puts it this way). A house voice: a startup app (casual, warm, short sentences, contractions, you / we, light humour) vs a bank (calm, confident, precise, no jokes, still plain English). Consistency: don't jump from chatty to bureaucratic (hereby, herein, pursuant to) or from formal to slang (Awesome, right?) inside one text. Rhythm: read it aloud; vary sentence length (known from c2-grammar-for-style, apply it, don't re-teach); end the sentence and the paragraph on the strong word (move weak tails like to be honest, I think, as well to the front or cut them). Precise verbs over adverb + weak verb: walked slowly (relaxed) → strolled / ambled; walked slowly (tired, heavy) → trudged; walked with firm steps → marched; said quietly → whispered / murmured; looked for a long time → stared (often surprise or rudeness) / gazed (admiration, dreaminess); rose sharply → soared; fell sharply → plunged / plummeted. Clichés to cut: at the end of the day, think outside the box, in today's fast-paced world (the English twin of 'Di era globalisasi ini'), last but not least, game-changer, it goes without saying. Replace with a fact or delete.

Objective rewrite-for-reader. Go beyond c1-register's three versions of one message: change CONTENT and ORDER, not just greeting and verbs. Ask: who reads it, what do they already know, what is their first question, what must they do or feel, where will they read it (a push notification has about 100 characters). Model: one payment-app outage (BayarKu, Friday 19:10–21:05) for customers (short, warm, apology, money is safe, what happens next), the CEO (bottom line first: duration, how many transactions, money lost or not, cause in one line, next step), engineers (technical cause, timeline, actions, no apology needed), a press statement (formal, third person, accountable, a quotable line from a named person, no blame on staff or suppliers). A price rise: loyal members (thanks, the new price, the reason, what stays the same, notice) vs investors (numbers, revenue and margin, churn = members who leave). Common error: sending the same text to everyone with only the greeting changed.

Grading and limits: at C2 tone and voice are matters of style, so accept any version that fits the stated reader and purpose and only mark clear cases wrong (a passive-aggressive or defensive phrase, a word that clearly breaks the stated voice, technical detail in a customer notification, a verb with the wrong mood: strolled for an exhausted person). For tone words, accept close synonyms of the list word with partial credit (annoyed for irritated). Explain the effect of a choice rather than calling it 'wrong English'. All brand messages, stories and statements are original practice texts; don't quote real style guides, ads or press releases beyond a few words. The audio is one plain voice: tone here is in the words, never in how something sounds. Contexts: Jakarta and Bandung startups, banks, an online shop, a coffee chain, a gym chain in Surabaya, a ministry, international clients.

keyPoints.title: Tone has dials: set them, and avoid tone that backfires
keyPoints.explanation: Tone is your attitude to the reader and the subject. Think of five dials: formal–casual, warm–cool, confident–tentative, serious–playful, direct–indirect. You move them with levers: word choice, sentence length, contractions, pronouns (we / you or 'the company'), hedges (perhaps, just, might) and punctuation (! or a dash). Watch for tone that backfires: a defensive apology (We're sorry you feel …, However, as clearly stated …) and passive-aggressive phrases (As per my last email = I already told you; Just a gentle reminder, the second time = you're late and I'm annoyed).

examples.en: Please be advised that your request has been declined.
examples.id: Dengan ini diberitahukan bahwa permintaan Anda ditolak. (dingin, formal, tidak personal)

examples.en: I'm sorry, but we can't approve your request this time. Here's what you can do next.
examples.id: Maaf, kali ini kami belum bisa menyetujui permintaanmu. Ini langkah yang bisa kamu ambil. (hangat, langsung)

examples.en: As per my last email, the figures are due today.
examples.id: Seperti yang sudah saya sampaikan di email sebelumnya, angkanya harus masuk hari ini. (pasif-agresif: 'aku sudah bilang')

id.title: Nada punya beberapa 'kenop': atur, dan hindari nada yang jadi bumerang
id.explanation: Nada (tone) adalah sikapmu terhadap pembaca dan topiknya. Bayangkan lima kenop: formal–santai, hangat–dingin, yakin–ragu, serius–jenaka, langsung–tidak langsung. Kamu menggesernya dengan 'tuas': pilihan kata, panjang kalimat, bentuk singkat (contraction), kata ganti (we / you atau 'the company'), kata pelunak (perhaps, just, might) dan tanda baca (! atau tanda pisah). Hati-hati dengan nada yang jadi bumerang: permintaan maaf yang defensif (We're sorry you feel …, However, as clearly stated …) dan frasa pasif-agresif (As per my last email = aku sudah bilang; Just a gentle reminder, yang kedua kalinya = kamu terlambat dan aku kesal).

keyPoints.title: One voice, steady rhythm, precise words
keyPoints.explanation: Voice is the personality that stays the same (a startup app sounds casual and warm, a bank calm and precise); tone shifts with the situation. Keep one voice through a text: don't jump from chatty to bureaucratic (hereby, pursuant to) or from formal to slang (Awesome, right?). Read your text aloud, vary sentence length and end on the strong word. Choose a precise verb instead of a weak verb + adverb (strolled, not walked slowly and happily; trudged, not walked slowly and tiredly), and cut clichés like at the end of the day.

examples.en: Your card's on its way. Tap Activate when it arrives, and you're good to go.
examples.id: Kartumu sedang dikirim. Ketuk Activate saat sampai, dan kamu siap memakainya. (suara aplikasi startup: santai, hangat)

examples.en: Your new card has been sent and should arrive within five working days.
examples.id: Kartu baru Anda telah dikirim dan akan tiba dalam lima hari kerja. (suara bank: tenang, tepat)

examples.en: After the night shift, Sari trudged home through the rain.
examples.id: Setelah sif malam, Sari berjalan pulang dengan langkah berat di tengah hujan. (trudged = lambat, berat, capek)

id.title: Satu suara, ritme yang terjaga, kata yang tepat
id.explanation: Suara (voice) adalah kepribadian tulisan yang tetap sama (aplikasi startup terdengar santai dan hangat, bank tenang dan tepat); nada (tone) berubah sesuai situasi. Jaga satu suara dari awal sampai akhir: jangan melompat dari gaya ngobrol ke gaya birokrasi (hereby, pursuant to) atau dari formal ke bahasa gaul (Awesome, right?). Bacakan tulisanmu dengan suara keras, variasikan panjang kalimat dan akhiri dengan kata yang kuat. Pilih kata kerja yang tepat daripada kata kerja lemah + kata keterangan (strolled, bukan walked slowly and happily; trudged, bukan walked slowly and tiredly), dan buang klise seperti at the end of the day.

keyPoints.title: The same message for different readers
keyPoints.explanation: Rewriting for a new reader means changing the content and its order, not just the greeting. Ask: who reads it, what do they already know, what is their first question, and what must they do or feel? One payment-app outage: customers need an apology, 'your money is safe' and what happens next; the CEO needs the impact in two lines; engineers need the technical cause and the actions; a press statement needs formal, accountable sentences and a quote from a named person.

examples.en: Sorry, payments aren't working right now. Your money is safe, and we're fixing it.
examples.id: Maaf, pembayaran sedang tidak bisa dilakukan. Uangmu aman, dan kami sedang memperbaikinya. (untuk pelanggan: notifikasi aplikasi)

examples.en: Payments were down for two hours on Friday: about 48,000 failed transactions, no money lost.
examples.id: Pembayaran mati dua jam pada hari Jumat: sekitar 48.000 transaksi gagal, tidak ada uang yang hilang. (untuk CEO: dampaknya dulu)

examples.en: Migration 412 locked the transactions table at 19:10; rollback completed at 20:52.
examples.id: Migrasi 412 mengunci tabel transaksi pukul 19.10; rollback selesai pukul 20.52. (untuk engineer: penyebab teknis)

id.title: Pesan yang sama untuk pembaca yang berbeda
id.explanation: Menulis ulang untuk pembaca baru berarti mengubah isi dan urutannya, bukan hanya salamnya. Tanyakan: siapa yang membaca, apa yang sudah mereka tahu, apa pertanyaan pertama mereka, dan apa yang harus mereka lakukan atau rasakan? Satu gangguan aplikasi pembayaran: pelanggan perlu permintaan maaf, 'uangmu aman' dan langkah berikutnya; CEO perlu dampaknya dalam dua baris; engineer perlu penyebab teknis dan tindakan; siaran pers perlu kalimat formal yang bertanggung jawab dan kutipan dari orang yang disebut namanya.

guidedPractice.prompt: A bank in Jakarta writes to a customer: 'Please be advised that your application has been declined.' On the warm–cool dial, is this warm or cool? Answer in one word.
guidedPractice.hint: Look at the levers: no 'we', no 'sorry', no reason, the passive, and the stiff 'Please be advised'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Make this sound confident for a proposal to your director. Remove the hedges and write the sentence: 'I just think we should maybe perhaps launch in March.'
expected: i think we should launch in march
i recommend that we launch in march
guidedPractice.hint: Just, maybe and perhaps all lower your confidence. One hedge can be polite; three sound unsure. Keep the core: we should launch in March.

guidedPractice.prompt: Pak Hasan has already sent two reminders about a contract. His third email begins: 'Not sure if you saw my previous emails …'. What is he really saying? Answer in a few words.
expected: i am annoyed you have not replied
guidedPractice.hint: After two reminders he is not really unsure. This is a polite surface over a complaint: what has the reader not done?

guidedPractice.prompt: Replace 'said very quietly' with ONE precise verb in the past tense: ''Not now,' she said very quietly, so the baby wouldn't wake up.'
guidedPractice.hint: A verb that already contains 'very quietly'. It starts with wh- (or try m-).

guidedPractice.prompt: Cut the cliché and keep the meaning: 'At the end of the day, the budget is the real problem.' Write the new sentence.
expected: the budget is the real problem
in the end the budget is the real problem
ultimately the budget is the real problem
the real problem is the budget
guidedPractice.hint: 'At the end of the day' adds nothing here. Delete it, or use one plain word like 'ultimately'.

independentPractice.prompt: An online shop's warehouse in Bandung is closed on Friday for a flood clean-up, so orders will be one day late. Write a short app notification (one or two sentences) for customers.
expected: sorry your order will arrive one day late because our bandung warehouse is closed for a flood clean-up
heads-up our bandung warehouse is closed on friday after a flood so your order will arrive a day late sorry
sorry orders from bandung will be one day late our warehouse is closed on friday for a flood clean-up
your order will arrive one day late because of a flood at our bandung warehouse we're sorry
sorry for the wait your order will arrive a day later than planned because our warehouse is closed after a flood
independentPractice.hint: Customers want to know: what happens to MY order? Start there, say sorry, give the reason in a few words. No internal details.

independentPractice.prompt: After a system outage, who needs the exact technical cause (which server, which change, what time) most: customers, the CEO or the engineers? Answer in one word.
independentPractice.hint: Who has to fix it and stop it happening again?

independentPractice.prompt: Bank Arta writes in a calm, professional voice. Which word breaks the voice? 'Dear Mr Tan, your new credit limit is Rp 50,000,000. Awesome, right? It takes effect on 1 November.' Write the word.
independentPractice.hint: Find the word that belongs in a chat with a friend, not in a letter from a bank.

assessment.prompt:
Read this practice email from a project manager in Jakarta, sent the day after a deadline:
'Hi Dimas,
Just a gentle reminder (again) that the report was due yesterday. As I'm sure you're aware, the client is waiting. Thanks in advance.'
Which word best describes its tone: grateful, irritated, apologetic or uncertain? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: irritated (polite words cover annoyance: '(again)', 'Just a gentle reminder' after a missed deadline, 'As I'm sure you're aware' = you should know this, and 'Thanks in advance' = I expect it done). A synonym not from the list (annoyed, frustrated, impatient, passive-aggressive) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (kesal, jengkel) = 60. 'grateful' = 0 (the literal meaning of 'thanks'; the email thanks no one for anything done). 'apologetic' = 0 (nobody apologises). 'uncertain' = 0 (the writer is completely sure the report is late).

assessment.prompt:
A customer in Surabaya complains that her order arrived five days late. The online shop replies:
'We're sorry you feel that the delivery was slow. However, as clearly stated on our website, all delivery times are estimates.'
Which word best describes the tone of this reply: sincere, defensive, playful or tentative? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: defensive ('sorry you feel' apologises for her feelings, not for the delay; 'However' cancels the apology; 'as clearly stated' suggests she didn't read the website). A synonym not from the list (dismissive, blaming, unapologetic, cold) = 80. The idea in Indonesian (defensif, membela diri) = 60. 'sincere' = 0 (it contains 'sorry' but takes no responsibility). 'playful' = 0 (nothing is light or joking). 'tentative' = 0 (there are no hedges; the shop is firm).

assessment.prompt: Rina, an account manager in Bandung, replies to a client who has reported a serious bug: 'Thanks for flagging this!!! We'll fix it today!!!' Her manager says one punctuation habit makes the reply sound unprofessional and almost cheerful about the client's problem. Which punctuation mark is it? Write its name in English.
assessment.rubric: Correct: the exclamation mark (American English: exclamation point). '!!!' reads as excitement or shouting; about a client's serious problem it sounds cheerful or careless. Better: 'Thanks for flagging this. We'll fix it today.' Just 'exclamation' = 80. The idea in Indonesian (tanda seru) = 60. 'full stop' / 'period' / 'comma' = 0 (not in the message, or not the problem).

assessment.prompt:
Jajan, a food delivery app in Jakarta, writes in a friendly, casual voice. Read this practice message:
'Hey Budi! Your new Jajan card is on its way 🎉 It should land in your mailbox by Friday. Once it arrives, tap Activate in the app and the aforementioned card is ready to go. Questions? Just ping us in the chat.'
Which ONE word breaks the voice? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: aforementioned (a legal, bureaucratic word in the middle of a chatty message; the voice needs 'your card' or just 'it'). 'aforementioned card' = 100. 'ping' = 0 (informal, it fits the casual voice). 'Hey' = 0 (fits the voice). 'Activate' = 0 (the name of a button). Any other word = 0.

assessment.prompt: A practice short story set in Yogyakarta: 'On Sunday evening, Pak Budi walked slowly and happily along Malioboro, enjoying the lights.' The editor asks you to replace 'walked slowly and happily' with ONE precise verb in the past tense. Write the verb.
assessment.rubric: Correct: strolled (walked slowly, relaxed, for pleasure). 'ambled' or 'sauntered' = 100. 'wandered' or 'meandered' = 70 (relaxed, but they suggest no clear direction rather than enjoyment). The right verb in the present tense (strolls) or base form (stroll) = 60. 'walked' = 20 (correct English, but the precise meaning is lost). 'trudged' = 0 (slow but tired and heavy: the wrong mood). 'marched', 'rushed', 'hurried' = 0 (the wrong speed or mood).

assessment.prompt:
An online shop in Jakarta had a problem with its checkout. Read this practice version of the update:
'Incident summary: the checkout service returned 503 errors from 14:02 to 14:47 after a config change set the connection-pool limit above what the database allows. Rolled back at 14:41. Action: add a limit check to the deploy pipeline.'
Who is this version written for: customers, the CEO, engineers or journalists? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: engineers (technical cause, an error code, config and pipeline words, exact times and an action for the team that fixes it). 'developers' or 'the tech team' = 100. 'the CEO' = 20 (it is short, but a CEO needs the impact: how many orders failed, money, customers; '503 errors' and 'connection-pool limit' mean little to most CEOs). 'customers' = 0 (no apology, nothing about their orders). 'journalists' = 0 (no formal statement, no quote, internal jargon).

assessment.prompt:
FitKota, a gym chain in Surabaya, is raising its monthly membership fee. Read this practice version:
'From 1 March, the monthly fee rises from Rp 300,000 to Rp 350,000. We expect this to add around Rp 4 billion to annual revenue, with member churn staying under 3%.'
Who is this version written for: loyal members, investors or the front-desk staff? Write the reader.
assessment.rubric: Correct: investors (it talks about annual revenue and churn, the share of members who leave: what investors care about). 'shareholders' = 100. 'the board' = 80. 'loyal members' = 0 (no thanks, no reason for the rise, nothing about what stays the same, and members don't want to read about how much more money the gym will make from them). 'front-desk staff' = 20 (they need the new price, but this version says nothing about what they should do or tell members).

material.title: Tone has dials, and levers that move them

id.title: Nada punya kenop, dan tuas untuk menggesernya

blocks.text:
Quick recap: you can already shift a message between **formal, neutral and informal** (register), choose words for their **feeling** (*slim* or *skinny*: connotation), vary sentence length for rhythm, and decode the polite code (*I'm not sure that's the best idea* = I disagree).

Now the C2 step. **Tone** (nada tulisan) is your attitude to the reader and the subject, and formality is only one part of it. Think of **five dials**:
- **formal ↔ casual**: *We are unable to …* / *We can't …*
- **warm ↔ cool**: *Thanks so much for your patience* / *Please be advised that …*
- **confident ↔ tentative**: *We recommend …* / *We were wondering if maybe …*
- **serious ↔ playful**: a plain statement / a light joke or an emoji
- **direct ↔ indirect**: *Please send it by 3 p.m.* / *It would be great to have it this afternoon.*

You turn the dials with **levers**:
- **word choice**: *help* or *assist*, *problem* or *issue*, *sorry* or *we regret*
- **sentence length**: short = brisk and confident; long = careful, sometimes cold
- **contractions** (bentuk singkat: *we're*, *can't*): warmer and more casual
- **pronouns**: *we* and *you* sound human; *the company*, *customers* and the passive sound distant
- **hedges** (kata pelunak: *perhaps, might, just, I was wondering*): one is polite, many sound unsure
- **punctuation**: one *!* is friendly; *!!!* is shouting or childish at work; a **dash** (—) adds a conversational aside; *…* sounds hesitant or reluctant

id.text:
Ulang singkat: kamu sudah bisa menggeser pesan antara **formal, netral dan informal** (register), memilih kata dari **rasanya** (*slim* atau *skinny*: konotasi), memvariasikan panjang kalimat untuk ritme, dan membaca kode sopan (*I'm not sure that's the best idea* = aku tidak setuju).

Sekarang langkah C2. **Nada** (tone) adalah sikapmu terhadap pembaca dan topiknya, dan tingkat formalitas hanya salah satu bagiannya. Bayangkan **lima kenop**:
- **formal ↔ santai**: *We are unable to …* / *We can't …*
- **hangat ↔ dingin**: *Thanks so much for your patience* / *Please be advised that …*
- **yakin ↔ ragu-ragu**: *We recommend …* / *We were wondering if maybe …*
- **serius ↔ jenaka**: pernyataan biasa / sedikit candaan atau emoji
- **langsung ↔ tidak langsung**: *Please send it by 3 p.m.* / *It would be great to have it this afternoon.*

Kamu memutar kenop itu dengan **tuas**:
- **pilihan kata**: *help* atau *assist*, *problem* atau *issue*, *sorry* atau *we regret*
- **panjang kalimat**: pendek = tegas dan yakin; panjang = hati-hati, kadang terasa dingin
- **bentuk singkat** (contraction: *we're*, *can't*): lebih hangat dan santai
- **kata ganti**: *we* dan *you* terdengar manusiawi; *the company*, *customers* dan kalimat pasif terdengar berjarak
- **kata pelunak** (hedge: *perhaps, might, just, I was wondering*): satu itu sopan, banyak terdengar tidak yakin
- **tanda baca**: satu *!* itu ramah; *!!!* terkesan berteriak atau kekanak-kanakan di tempat kerja; **tanda pisah** (—) menambahkan selipan seperti mengobrol; *…* terdengar ragu atau enggan

rows.en: The meeting has been moved to Thursday.
rows.id: Rapatnya dipindah ke hari Kamis.
rows.note: cool, neutral: the passive, no people

id.note: dingin, netral: kalimat pasif, tanpa orang

rows.en: Quick heads-up: we've moved the meeting to Thursday. Hope that still works for you!
rows.id: Info singkat: rapatnya kami pindah ke Kamis. Semoga masih bisa ya!
rows.note: warm, casual: we / you, a contraction, one !

id.note: hangat, santai: we / you, bentuk singkat, satu !

rows.en: Would it perhaps be possible to move the meeting to Thursday?
rows.id: Apakah kira-kira rapatnya bisa dipindah ke Kamis?
rows.note: tentative, indirect: a question and a hedge

id.note: ragu-ragu, tidak langsung: pertanyaan dan kata pelunak

rows.en: Let's meet on Thursday instead.
rows.id: Kita ketemu hari Kamis saja.
rows.note: confident, direct: short, no hedge

id.note: yakin, langsung: pendek, tanpa pelunak

blocks.text:
**Indonesian trap: no particles in English.** Indonesian sets the tone with little words: *Tolong dikirim **ya***, *Kok belum **sih**?*, *Ayo **dong***. English has none of them, so learners often reach for *!!!*, emoji or *Kindly …* instead. Use the levers: *Could you send it today?* (polite, warm) is the English version of *Tolong dikirim hari ini ya*, not *Please send it today!!!*.

**Second trap: sungkan hedges.** Stacking polite words (*I just wanted to maybe ask if possibly …*) feels respectful in Indonesian, but in English it makes a good proposal sound unsure. Keep one hedge, then say it clearly.

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: bahasa Inggris tidak punya partikel.** Bahasa Indonesia mengatur nada dengan kata-kata kecil: *Tolong dikirim **ya***, *Kok belum **sih**?*, *Ayo **dong***. Bahasa Inggris tidak punya kata-kata itu, jadi pelajar sering memakai *!!!*, emoji atau *Kindly …* sebagai gantinya. Pakai tuasnya: *Could you send it today?* (sopan, hangat) adalah versi Inggris dari *Tolong dikirim hari ini ya*, bukan *Please send it today!!!*.

**Jebakan kedua: pelunak karena sungkan.** Menumpuk kata sopan (*I just wanted to maybe ask if possibly …*) terasa hormat dalam bahasa Indonesia, tapi dalam bahasa Inggris membuat usulan yang bagus terdengar tidak yakin. Pakai satu pelunak, lalu katakan dengan jelas.

blocks.prompt: Which lever makes 'We regret that the service is unavailable' sound cooler than 'Sorry, we're down right now'?
options: Only the length of the sentence.
Formal words, no contraction and 'the service' instead of 'we'.
blocks.explain: Several levers work together: *regret* and *unavailable* are formal, there's no contraction (compare *we're*), and *the service* puts a thing, not people, at the centre. There's no exclamation mark in either sentence, and the lengths are almost the same.

id.prompt: Tuas mana yang membuat 'We regret that the service is unavailable' terdengar lebih dingin daripada 'Sorry, we're down right now'?
id.explain: Beberapa tuas bekerja bersama: *regret* dan *unavailable* itu kata formal, tidak ada bentuk singkat seperti *we're*, dan *the service* menaruh benda, bukan orang, di tengah kalimat. Tidak ada tanda seru di kedua kalimat, dan panjangnya hampir sama.

material.title: When tone backfires: defensive apologies and passive-aggressive reminders

id.title: Saat nada jadi bumerang: maaf yang defensif dan pengingat pasif-agresif

blocks.text:
A **tone mismatch** happens when the words say one thing and the tone says another. Two kinds do real damage at work.

**1. The defensive apology.** It contains *sorry* but takes no responsibility:
- *We're sorry **you feel** the delivery was slow.* (sorry for your feelings, not for the delay)
- *We apologise **if** anyone was inconvenienced.* (maybe nobody was)
- *…**However, as clearly stated** on our website, …* (*however* cancels the apology; *clearly stated* means 'you didn't read it')
A real apology names the problem, owns it and says what you'll do: *We're sorry your order arrived five days late. That was our mistake, and we've refunded the delivery fee.*

**2. Passive-aggressive phrases** (pasif-agresif: marah, tapi disamarkan dengan kata-kata sopan). Literally polite; many readers hear the sting:
- *As per my last email, …* = I already told you; read your emails.
- *Just a gentle reminder …* / *Friendly reminder …* (the second time, or after a deadline) = You're late, and I'm annoyed.
- *Not sure if you saw my previous email …* = You ignored me.
- *As I'm sure you're aware, …* = You should know this.
- *Going forward, please …* = Don't do that again.
- *Thanks in advance.* = I expect you to do this.
These are **tendencies**, not rules: some people use them innocently. But a C2 writer chooses them only when the sting is intended. The fix is **neutral and specific**: *Could you send the figures by 3 p.m.? I need them for the board pack.*

id.text:
**Ketidakcocokan nada** terjadi saat kata-katanya mengatakan satu hal dan nadanya mengatakan hal lain. Dua jenis ini benar-benar merusak di tempat kerja.

**1. Permintaan maaf yang defensif.** Ada kata *sorry*, tapi tidak mengambil tanggung jawab:
- *We're sorry **you feel** the delivery was slow.* (minta maaf atas perasaanmu, bukan atas keterlambatannya)
- *We apologise **if** anyone was inconvenienced.* (seolah-olah mungkin tidak ada yang dirugikan)
- *…**However, as clearly stated** on our website, …* (*however* membatalkan permintaan maafnya; *clearly stated* berarti 'kamu tidak membacanya')
Permintaan maaf yang sungguhan menyebut masalahnya, mengakuinya dan mengatakan apa yang akan dilakukan: *We're sorry your order arrived five days late. That was our mistake, and we've refunded the delivery fee.*

**2. Frasa pasif-agresif** (marah, tapi disamarkan dengan kata-kata sopan). Secara harfiah sopan; banyak pembaca merasakan 'sindirannya':
- *As per my last email, …* = Aku sudah bilang; baca email-mu.
- *Just a gentle reminder …* / *Friendly reminder …* (yang kedua kalinya, atau setelah tenggat lewat) = Kamu terlambat, dan aku kesal.
- *Not sure if you saw my previous email …* = Kamu mengabaikanku.
- *As I'm sure you're aware, …* = Harusnya kamu sudah tahu.
- *Going forward, please …* = Jangan ulangi lagi.
- *Thanks in advance.* = Aku berharap ini kamu kerjakan.
Ini **kecenderungan**, bukan aturan: sebagian orang memakainya tanpa maksud apa-apa. Tapi penulis C2 memakainya hanya kalau sindirannya memang disengaja. Solusinya **netral dan spesifik**: *Could you send the figures by 3 p.m.? I need them for the board pack.*

blocks.text:
**Indonesian traps.** Many Indonesian writers use *as per* as neutral formal English (from *sesuai dengan*). *As per the contract* is fine; **As per my last email** carries the same sting as *Seperti yang sudah saya sampaikan sebelumnya*. And *Mohon maaf atas ketidaknyamanannya* translated as *We apologise for any inconvenience* sounds like a template: name the actual problem instead.

*Sekadar mengingatkan* is a normal, kind phrase in Indonesian, and a first, neutral reminder in English is fine too. It's the repeated or late *gentle reminder* that readers hear as irritation.

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia.** Banyak penulis Indonesia memakai *as per* sebagai bahasa Inggris formal yang netral (dari *sesuai dengan*). *As per the contract* tidak masalah; **As per my last email** punya sindiran yang sama dengan *Seperti yang sudah saya sampaikan sebelumnya*. Lalu *Mohon maaf atas ketidaknyamanannya* yang diterjemahkan menjadi *We apologise for any inconvenience* terdengar seperti template: sebutkan masalahnya yang sebenarnya.

*Sekadar mengingatkan* adalah frasa yang wajar dan ramah dalam bahasa Indonesia, dan pengingat pertama yang netral dalam bahasa Inggris juga tidak masalah. Yang terbaca sebagai kesal adalah *gentle reminder* yang diulang-ulang atau dikirim setelah terlambat.

options: We're sorry if you were unhappy with your stay.
We're sorry the air conditioning in your room didn't work. We've refunded one night.
We're sorry you feel the room was too hot. However, all rooms are checked daily.
blocks.explain: It names the problem (*the air conditioning didn't work*) and says what was done (a refund). *Sorry if you were unhappy* doubts the problem, and *sorry you feel … However …* blames the guest's feelings and then defends the hotel.

id.prompt: Permintaan maaf mana yang mengambil tanggung jawab?
id.explain: Kalimat itu menyebut masalahnya (*the air conditioning didn't work*) dan apa yang sudah dilakukan (pengembalian uang). *Sorry if you were unhappy* meragukan masalahnya, dan *sorry you feel … However …* menyalahkan perasaan tamunya lalu membela hotelnya.

material.title: One voice: house style, consistency and precise words

id.title: Satu suara: gaya rumah, konsistensi dan kata yang tepat

blocks.text:
**Voice** (suara tulisan) is the personality that stays the same; **tone** shifts with the situation. A good brand keeps one voice and adjusts its tone: the same app is playful in a welcome message and calm and serious when your payment fails.

A **house voice** (gaya rumah: the style a company always writes in) depends on who the company wants to be:
- a **startup app**: casual and warm, short sentences, contractions, *you* and *we*, a little humour
- a **bank**: calm, confident and precise, no jokes, but still plain English (not legal language)

The C2 skill is **keeping one voice through the whole text**. A chatty message that suddenly says *hereby* or *pursuant to* (birokratis), or a bank letter that suddenly says *Awesome, right?* (bahasa gaul), sounds as if two people wrote it. Check every word against the voice.

**Precise words.** A weak verb + an adverb (kata keterangan, like *slowly, quietly*) is often one precise verb in disguise:
- *walked slowly* (relaxed, for pleasure) → **strolled**, *ambled*
- *walked slowly* (tired, heavy steps) → **trudged**
- *walked with firm, strong steps* → **marched**
- *said very quietly* → **whispered**, *murmured*
- *looked for a long time* → **stared** (surprise, often rude) / **gazed** (admiration, dreaming)
- *rose / fell very sharply* → **soared** / **plunged**, *plummeted*
The precise verb is shorter **and** tells the reader the mood.

id.text:
**Suara** (voice) adalah kepribadian tulisan yang tetap sama; **nada** (tone) berubah sesuai situasi. Merek yang baik menjaga satu suara dan menyesuaikan nadanya: aplikasi yang sama terdengar jenaka di pesan sambutan, tapi tenang dan serius saat pembayaranmu gagal.

**Gaya rumah** (house voice: gaya tulisan yang selalu dipakai sebuah perusahaan) bergantung pada ingin jadi apa perusahaan itu:
- **aplikasi startup**: santai dan hangat, kalimat pendek, bentuk singkat, *you* dan *we*, sedikit humor
- **bank**: tenang, yakin dan tepat, tanpa candaan, tapi tetap bahasa Inggris yang sederhana (bukan bahasa hukum)

Keterampilan C2-nya adalah **menjaga satu suara di seluruh tulisan**. Pesan santai yang tiba-tiba memakai *hereby* atau *pursuant to* (birokratis), atau surat bank yang tiba-tiba berkata *Awesome, right?* (bahasa gaul), terdengar seperti ditulis dua orang. Periksa setiap kata: cocok dengan suaranya atau tidak.

**Kata yang tepat.** Kata kerja lemah + kata keterangan (adverb, seperti *slowly, quietly*) sering kali adalah satu kata kerja yang tepat yang sedang 'menyamar':
- *walked slowly* (santai, untuk menikmati) → **strolled**, *ambled*
- *walked slowly* (capek, langkah berat) → **trudged**
- *walked with firm, strong steps* → **marched**
- *said very quietly* → **whispered**, *murmured*
- *looked for a long time* → **stared** (kaget, sering tidak sopan) / **gazed** (kagum, melamun)
- *rose / fell very sharply* → **soared** / **plunged**, *plummeted*
Kata kerja yang tepat lebih pendek **dan** memberi tahu pembaca suasananya.

blocks.text: **Cut clichés.** A cliché (klise) is a phrase used so often that readers skip it: *at the end of the day*, *think outside the box*, *in today's fast-paced world* (the English twin of *Di era globalisasi ini*), *last but not least*, *a game-changer*, *it goes without saying*. Delete it, or replace it with a fact: not *a game-changer for farmers*, but *it cuts the time to sell a harvest from three days to one*.

id.text: **Buang klise.** Klise adalah frasa yang terlalu sering dipakai sampai pembaca melewatinya: *at the end of the day*, *think outside the box*, *in today's fast-paced world* (kembaran Inggris dari *Di era globalisasi ini*), *last but not least*, *a game-changer*, *it goes without saying*. Hapus, atau ganti dengan fakta: bukan *a game-changer for farmers*, tapi *it cuts the time to sell a harvest from three days to one*.

blocks.prompt: A bank's message says: 'Your loan has been approved. The funds will be transferred within two working days. Easy peasy! Your first repayment is due on 5 December.' Which part breaks the bank's voice?
blocks.explain: *Easy peasy* is childish slang (gampang banget) in the middle of a calm, precise message. The other two parts are exactly the kind of clear, exact information a bank's voice gives.

id.prompt: Pesan sebuah bank: 'Your loan has been approved. The funds will be transferred within two working days. Easy peasy! Your first repayment is due on 5 December.' Bagian mana yang merusak suara bank itu?
id.explain: *Easy peasy* adalah bahasa gaul yang kekanak-kanakan (gampang banget) di tengah pesan yang tenang dan tepat. Dua bagian lainnya adalah informasi jelas dan tepat yang memang khas suara bank.

material.title: Rhythm: read it aloud, end on the strong word

id.title: Ritme: bacakan, akhiri dengan kata yang kuat

blocks.text:
You already vary sentence length and put a short sentence after long ones. Three more habits give writing a steady rhythm:
- **Read it aloud.** Where you run out of breath, split the sentence. Where every sentence has the same length and shape, it sounds like a machine: change one.
- **End on the strong word.** The end of a sentence is the spotlight (end-focus). Don't leave a weak tail there: *The results were disappointing, to be honest.* → *To be honest, the results were disappointing.* *We need your support now, I think.* → *I think we need your support now.*
- **End the paragraph strongly too.** Finish on the point you want remembered, not on a detail or a polite extra (*…, etc.*, *…as well*).

Rhythm also keeps the voice consistent: a casual voice has more short sentences; a formal voice has longer ones, but it still needs a short one now and then.

id.text:
Kamu sudah memvariasikan panjang kalimat dan menaruh kalimat pendek setelah kalimat-kalimat panjang. Tiga kebiasaan lagi membuat ritme tulisan terjaga:
- **Bacakan dengan suara keras.** Di mana napasmu habis, pecah kalimatnya. Kalau setiap kalimat punya panjang dan bentuk yang sama, tulisannya terdengar seperti mesin: ubah satu.
- **Akhiri dengan kata yang kuat.** Akhir kalimat adalah 'lampu sorot' (end-focus). Jangan tinggalkan ekor yang lemah di sana: *The results were disappointing, to be honest.* → *To be honest, the results were disappointing.* *We need your support now, I think.* → *I think we need your support now.*
- **Akhiri paragraf dengan kuat juga.** Tutup dengan poin yang ingin diingat, bukan dengan detail atau tambahan basa-basi (*…, etc.*, *…as well*).

Ritme juga menjaga suara tetap konsisten: suara santai punya lebih banyak kalimat pendek; suara formal punya kalimat lebih panjang, tapi tetap butuh kalimat pendek sesekali.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence ends on the strong word?
options: The new clinic saved three lives in its first week, according to the hospital.
According to the hospital, the new clinic saved three lives in its first week.
The new clinic, according to the hospital, in its first week saved three lives.
blocks.explain: The source (*according to the hospital*) moves to the front, so the sentence ends on the news: *three lives in its first week*. The first version ends on the weak source; the third is broken up and awkward to read aloud.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang berakhir pada kata yang kuat?
id.explain: Sumbernya (*according to the hospital*) pindah ke depan, jadi kalimat berakhir pada beritanya: *three lives in its first week*. Versi pertama berakhir pada sumber yang lemah; versi ketiga terpotong-potong dan janggal saat dibacakan.

blocks.text:
In the register lesson you rewrote one message as formal, neutral and informal. Now go further: for a really different reader you change the **content** and its **order**, not only the greeting and the verbs. Ask four questions:
- **Who** reads it, and what do they already know?
- What is their **first question**? Answer it first.
- What must they **do or feel** after reading?
- **Where** will they read it? (A push notification shows about 100 characters.)

Here is one practice incident: the payment app **BayarKu** was down on Friday from 19:10 to 21:05. About 48,000 payments failed; no money was lost. The cause: a database update (migration 412) locked a table.

id.text:
Di pelajaran register kamu sudah menulis ulang satu pesan menjadi formal, netral dan informal. Sekarang lebih jauh: untuk pembaca yang benar-benar berbeda kamu mengubah **isi** dan **urutannya**, bukan hanya salam dan kata kerjanya. Ajukan empat pertanyaan:
- **Siapa** yang membaca, dan apa yang sudah mereka tahu?
- Apa **pertanyaan pertama** mereka? Jawab itu dulu.
- Apa yang harus mereka **lakukan atau rasakan** setelah membaca?
- **Di mana** mereka membacanya? (Notifikasi aplikasi hanya menampilkan sekitar 100 karakter.)

Ini satu contoh kejadian latihan: aplikasi pembayaran **BayarKu** mati pada hari Jumat pukul 19.10 sampai 21.05. Sekitar 48.000 pembayaran gagal; tidak ada uang yang hilang. Penyebabnya: pembaruan database (migrasi 412) mengunci sebuah tabel.

blocks.text:
**The commonest mistake:** sending the same text to everyone and changing only *Dear …* at the top. Customers don't need *migration 412*; engineers don't need *we're sorry we let people down*; the CEO doesn't need the whole timeline. Each reader gets the part they need, in their words, in the order of their questions.

The same goes for a **price rise**: loyal customers get thanks, the new price, the honest reason and what stays the same; investors get the numbers (revenue, margin, **churn** = the share of customers who leave).

id.text:
**Kesalahan paling umum:** mengirim teks yang sama ke semua orang dan hanya mengganti *Dear …* di atasnya. Pelanggan tidak perlu *migration 412*; engineer tidak perlu *we're sorry we let people down*; CEO tidak perlu seluruh kronologinya. Setiap pembaca mendapat bagian yang mereka perlukan, dengan kata-kata mereka, dalam urutan pertanyaan mereka.

Begitu juga untuk **kenaikan harga**: pelanggan setia mendapat ucapan terima kasih, harga baru, alasan yang jujur dan apa yang tetap sama; investor mendapat angkanya (pendapatan, margin, **churn** = persentase pelanggan yang berhenti).

blocks.prompt: Which sentence belongs in the version for the CEO?

Please add your notes to the incident doc before 10:00.
blocks.explain: A CEO's first question is the impact: how big was it, and did we lose money? The first sentence is for customers (it speaks to *your money*); the third is a task for the engineers.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang cocok untuk versi CEO?
id.explain: Pertanyaan pertama seorang CEO adalah dampaknya: seberapa besar, dan apakah ada uang yang hilang? Kalimat pertama untuk pelanggan (berbicara tentang *your money*); kalimat ketiga adalah tugas untuk para engineer.

Baca email latihan dari seorang manajer proyek di Jakarta ini, yang dikirim sehari setelah tenggat:
'Hi Dimas,
Just a gentle reminder (again) that the report was due yesterday. As I'm sure you're aware, the client is waiting. Thanks in advance.'
Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan nadanya: grateful, irritated, apologetic atau uncertain? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.sn-2:
Seorang pelanggan di Surabaya mengeluh pesanannya terlambat lima hari. Toko online itu membalas:
'We're sorry you feel that the delivery was slow. However, as clearly stated on our website, all delivery times are estimates.'
Kata mana yang paling tepat menggambarkan nada balasan ini: sincere, defensive, playful atau tentative? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.sn-3: Rina, seorang account manager di Bandung, membalas klien yang melaporkan bug serius: 'Thanks for flagging this!!! We'll fix it today!!!' Manajernya bilang ada satu kebiasaan tanda baca yang membuat balasan itu terdengar tidak profesional dan seolah-olah senang dengan masalah klien. Tanda baca apa itu? assessment.sn-4:
Jajan, aplikasi pesan-antar makanan di Jakarta, menulis dengan suara yang ramah dan santai. Baca pesan latihan ini:
'Hey Budi! Your new Jajan card is on its way 🎉 It should land in your mailbox by Friday. Once it arrives, tap Activate in the app and the aforementioned card is ready to go. Questions? Just ping us in the chat.'
SATU kata mana yang merusak suara itu? Tulis katanya.
assessment.sn-5: Sebuah cerita pendek latihan berlatar Yogyakarta: 'On Sunday evening, Pak Budi walked slowly and happily along Malioboro, enjoying the lights.' Editornya memintamu mengganti 'walked slowly and happily' dengan SATU kata kerja yang tepat dalam bentuk lampau (past tense). Tulis kata kerjanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.sn-6:
Sebuah toko online di Jakarta mengalami masalah di halaman pembayarannya. Baca versi latihan dari laporan ini:
'Incident summary: the checkout service returned 503 errors from 14:02 to 14:47 after a config change set the connection-pool limit above what the database allows. Rolled back at 14:41. Action: add a limit check to the deploy pipeline.'
Untuk siapa versi ini ditulis: customers, the CEO, engineers atau journalists? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.sn-7:
FitKota, jaringan pusat kebugaran di Surabaya, menaikkan iuran anggota bulanannya. Baca versi latihan ini:
'From 1 March, the monthly fee rises from Rp 300,000 to Rp 350,000. We expect this to add around Rp 4 billion to annual revenue, with member churn staying under 3%.'
Untuk siapa versi ini ditulis: loyal members, investors atau the front-desk staff? Tulis pembacanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
